summary: Three distribution lists for sending out Network documents such as RFCs, for sites, the NIC and station agents. These were postal addresses, not email lists. It replaced RFC 300 and was replaced by RFC 329.

plainLanguage.summary: An address list for who gets paper copies of network notes, replacing an earlier version.

questions: how were rfcs distributed early internet
subtitle: Three postal mailing lists for distributing network documents across ARPANET sites.

tldr.problem: ARPANET sites needed a standard way to distribute RFCs and network documents to liaisons, other participants, and station agents.
tldr.mechanism: Three mailing lists—A for liaisons, B for non-site participants, and C for station agents—define who receives documents and in what form.
tldr.outcome: A centralized distribution system ensured all network sites received necessary documentation through postal mail.

today: RFC 303 is Historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 329. It reflects the ARPANET's growing international reach and the organizational structure for document distribution before email became standard.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 303 establishes three distribution lists for ARPANET network documents such as RFCs. List A covers network liaisons and others who should receive initial distribution of RFCs whether sent from the Network Information Center (NIC) or from sites. List B is for the NIC to use when distributing documents to non-site participants. List C defines station agents who receive copies from NIC of all documents distributed to liaisons. The RFC notes that for phone numbers and lists by sites, see the Current Directory of Network Participants.
sections.plainLanguage: Three separate mailing lists said who to mail paper copies to: the first for the main contacts at each site, the second for people outside the network, and the third for mail handlers at each site.

sections.title: List A: Initial Distribution List
sections.content: List A includes network liaisons and others who should receive initial RFCs and selected catalogs from either NIC or directly from sites. Entries cover all major ARPANET sites: UCLA (NMC and CCN), SRI (NIC and AI), UCSB, Utah, BBN (three contacts), MIT (Multics and DM), Rand, SDC, Harvard, Lincoln (67 and TX2), Stanford, Illinois, Case, Carnegie, Ames, Paoli, and others. Each entry provides a contact name, site/organization, mailing address, and phone number. The RFC notes that all but local mail should be sent airmail.
sections.plainLanguage: A list of 30 network people at 20+ sites, with their mailing addresses and phone numbers, who should get every new network document.

sections.title: Lists B and C: Extended Distribution
sections.content: List B covers NIC distribution to non-site participants, including educational institutions (EDUCOM, universities), international sites (NPL, Neth, Canada), and research centers (MERIT, RADC, CCA). List C provides station agents at ARPANET sites who receive weekly (or more frequent) mailings of all documents distributed to liaisons. Station agents are secondary contacts at the same organizations, handling document receipt and distribution locally. The lists total approximately 70 contacts across 40+ organizations in North America and Europe.
sections.plainLanguage: Two more lists showed who else should get copies: universities and research centers that used the network, and helper contacts at each site who handled incoming mail.
